override.meaning: Wiktionary glosses فِي as “in, within” — the concept “in (inside a place)”; the check looks for the words “inside” / “place”, which its wording lacks.

profile.feeling: Being inside or at a place — the everyday “in” and “at”.

senses.def: at (a place: at home, at school, at work)
in (a month, a season, a year; a part of the day): فِي يَنَايِرَ, فِي الصَّيْفِ, فِي الصَّبَاحِ
at (a time of the clock): فِي السَّاعَةِ الْخَامِسَةِ (at five o’clock)
on (a day): فِي يَوْمِ الْجُمُعَةِ — or with no preposition: يَوْمَ الْجُمُعَةِ
about, concerning (after some verbs: فَكَّرَ فِي, to think about)
times, multiplied by: ثَلَاثَةٌ فِي أَرْبَعَةٍ (3 × 4)

examples.tr: The book is in the bag.
I live in a small village.
My father is at work.
We are at home.
I drink coffee in the morning.
We travel in the summer.
The lesson starts at eight o’clock.
The train arrives at five o’clock.
We don’t work on Friday.
My grandfather visits us on Saturday.

collocations.tr: in it (m. / f.); there is … in it

synonyms.nuance: in, at — بِالْبَيْتِ is literary or regional; the standard “in” is فِي
inside — stresses the interior: دَاخِلَ الْبَيْتِ

etymology.text: Wiktionary: possibly related to Proto-Semitic *pay- (“mouth, opening, entrance”) and *piʔat- (“side, front”); it took over functions of the old preposition *bV- (Arabic بِـ).

funFacts: Greek σε covers in, at and to; Arabic splits it: فِي for “in, at” (where?), إِلَى for “to” (where to?).
فِي also multiplies: ثَلَاثَةٌ فِي أَرْبَعَةٍ = three times four (Wiktionary).
pitfalls: Before al- the ī is shortened in speech (fi l-bayt), but the spelling stays فِي الْبَيْتِ.
With pronoun endings: فِيهِ, فِيهَا, فِيهِمْ (-hi, -him after ī) and فِيَّ (in me).
subtleties: Arabic does not distinguish “in” and “at” for places: فِي الْمَدْرَسَةِ = in school / at school. “At someone’s place” is عِنْدَ: عِنْدَ الطَّبِيبِ.
The noun after فِي is genitive: فِي بَيْتٍ (-in), فِي الْبَيْتِ (-i).
Time: one فِي for English at / on / in and German um / am / im — فِي السَّاعَةِ الْخَامِسَةِ (at five), فِي يَوْمِ الْأَحَدِ (on Sunday), فِي يَنَايِرَ, فِي الصَّيْفِ (in January, in summer).

profile.feeling: Movement towards: where to?

senses.def: until, to (in time): مِنَ الصَّبَاحِ إِلَى الْمَسَاءِ (from morning till evening)
until, till (time): مِنَ الصَّبَاحِ إِلَى الْمَسَاءِ

examples.tr: Where to? — Home.
I go to school every day.
I work from morning till evening.
I work from morning till evening.

examples.text: الْمَحَلُّ مَفْتُوحٌ مِنَ السَّاعَةِ التَّاسِعَةِ إِلَى السَّاعَةِ الْخَامِسَةِ.
examples.tr: The shop is open from nine to five.

synonyms.nuance: to, for — with persons and purposes; with places mostly in set phrases
towards — direction only, without arriving

etymology.text: From Proto-Semitic *ʾila (“towards, nigh”); Wiktionary compares عَلَى and the Semitic *la / *li of Arabic لِ.

funFacts: إِلَى اللِّقَاءِ (goodbye) is literally “until the meeting” — like German auf Wiedersehen and Greek εις το επανιδείν.
pitfalls: Written with ى but read -ā: ʾilā. With a pronoun the ى becomes يْ: إِلَيْكَ, إِلَيْهِ, إِلَيَّ (to me).
Not إِلَّا (ʾillā, “except”): إِلَى has a single l.
subtleties: إِلَى answers “where to?” (إِلَى أَيْنَ؟), فِي answers “where?” — but the noun is genitive after both: Arabic shows the direction with the preposition, not with the case (German: in die Schule / in der Schule).
In time, مِنْ … إِلَى … is “from … to / until …”; alone, “until” is usually حَتَّى (lesson 15).

profile.feeling: Origins and starting points: from.

senses.def: from (a place, a person, a time)
of, some of (a part of a whole): وَاحِدٌ مِنْهُمْ
than (after an elative: أَكْبَرُ مِنْ …, bigger than …)

examples.text: مِنْ أَيْنَ أَنْتَ؟ أَنَا مِنْ مِصْرَ.
examples.tr: Where are you from? — I’m from Egypt.
This bread is from the market.
One of my friends is a doctor.
My brother is older than me.
The train is faster than the bus.
I like tea more than coffee.

synonyms.nuance: away from, off — distance and separation: بَعِيدٌ عَنِ الْبَيْتِ
from someone’s place: مِنْ عِنْدِ الطَّبِيبِ

etymology.text: From Proto-West Semitic *min; cognate with Hebrew מִן (min) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Hebrew מִן (min) is the same word — and Hebrew shortens it to the prefix מִ־ (mi-): מִתֵּל אָבִיב, “from Tel Aviv”.
pitfalls: Before al- it is مِنَ (min-a): مِنَ الْبَيْتِ, not *مِنْ الْبَيْتِ.
Without vowels مِنْ (min, from) and مَنْ (man, who) look the same: من.
With pronoun endings the n doubles: مِنِّي (from me), مِنَّا (from us).
subtleties: مِنْ also marks “than” (أَكْبَرُ مِنِّي) and “part of” (بَعْضٌ مِنَ الْخُبْزِ).
For “than” Arabic uses the same مِنْ as “from”: أَكْبَرُ مِنِّي, “bigger from me” — exactly like Hebrew גָּדוֹל מִמֶּנִּי.

profile.feeling: Company and togetherness: with.

senses.def: with, together with (a person; something that goes along)
having on oneself: مَعِي (I have with me)

examples.tr: I’m with my friend at the café.
I drink tea with milk.
Do you have a pen on you?
And yet we love him.

synonyms.nuance: with — an instrument or an ingredient: قَهْوَةٌ بِالْحَلِيبِ, أَكْتُبُ بِالْقَلَمِ
in the company of

etymology.text: Cognate with Ugaritic mʿ and, with the consonants swapped, Hebrew עִם (ʿim) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Hebrew עִם (im) is the same word with its letters swapped (metathesis): مَعَ is m-ʿ, עִם is ʿ-m.
pitfalls: A tool is بِـ, not مَعَ: أَكْتُبُ بِالْقَلَمِ (I write with a pen). مَعَ is company: مَعَ صَدِيقِي.
مَعَ always ends in -a; before al- it is read maʿa l-…: مَعَ الْحَلِيبِ.
subtleties: مَعِي، مَعَكَ … = “I have on me, you have on you”: هَلْ مَعَكَ مَاءٌ؟ — what you carry now, unlike عِنْدِي (what you own).

profile.feeling: A tiny prefix with many jobs: with, by, in, for.

senses.def: with (an ingredient, a tool, a manner): قَهْوَةٌ بِالْحَلِيبِ

examples.tr: I drink coffee with milk.
I write with a pen.
How much is this?
We travel by train.

synonyms.nuance: with = together with (company)
by means of

etymology.text: Ultimately from Proto-Semitic *bV- (“with, in, at, among”); cognates Aramaic ב־, Classical Syriac ܒ-, Hebrew בְּ־ (bə-) and Geʿez በ (bä) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Hebrew בְּ־ (be-) is the same prefix — but in Hebrew it is the everyday “in” (בַּבַּיִת, at home), where Arabic uses فِي.
بِسْمِ اللّٰهِ, the opening words of the Qurʾān, start with this بِ.
pitfalls: بِ is always written together with the next word: بِالْحَلِيبِ, بِكَ — never alone.
With pronoun endings: بِهِ, بِهَا, بِهِمْ (-hi, -him after i).
subtleties: Dishes are named with بِ: أَرُزٌّ بِالدَّجَاجِ (rice with chicken), شَايٌ بِالنَّعْنَاعِ (mint tea).

profile.feeling: Leaving something out: without.

examples.tr: A coffee without sugar, please.
I don’t go out without my phone.
Life without you is hard.

synonyms.nuance: without — shorter and more formal (also “below, less than”)
without — the same meaning
without — before a bare noun: بِلَا سُكَّرٍ
without, other than

etymology.text: Compounded from the preposition بِ (bi-, “with”) + the preposition دُونَ (dūna, “below, short of, without”) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: The old preposition دُونَ meant “below, short of” — so “without” is literally “at short of”.
pitfalls: The noun after it is genitive: بِدُونِ سُكَّرٍ (-in), بِدُونِ الْحَلِيبِ (-i).
Written as one word: بِدُونِ.
subtleties: With pronoun endings: بِدُونِي (without me), بِدُونِكَ (without you).

profile.feeling: For whom, whose, to whom — the little lām.

senses.def: belonging to — هٰذَا لِي (this is mine)

examples.tr: This coffee is for you.
This bag is for my mother.
This book is mine.
Thank you (to a woman).

synonyms.nuance: for the sake of, for (a purpose)
for the sake of

etymology.text: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *lV- (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Hebrew לְ־ (le-) is the same prefix: יֵשׁ לִי (yesh li, “I have”) matches Arabic لِي, and לָכֶם (lakhem) matches لَكُمْ.
pitfalls: Its vowel changes with pronoun endings: لِي, but لَكَ, لَكِ, لَهُ, لَهَا, لَنَا (la-).
Before al- the alif of the article drops: لِلْبَيْتِ (li-l-bayti), not *لِالْبَيْتِ.
subtleties: Ownership: هٰذَا لِي = this is mine; لِي أَخٌ = I have a brother (relations, rights) — beside عِنْدِي.
Always written together with the next word: لِأُمِّي, لَكَ.

profile.feeling: Topics and distance: about, away from.

senses.def: away from, off (distance, separation): بَعِيدٌ عَنْ …
on the authority of, according to (reports)

examples.tr: We’re talking about work.
This is a book about Arab cooking.
What about you?
The airport is far from the city.

synonyms.nuance: about, around — a topic: كِتَابٌ حَوْلَ …
regarding, concerning

etymology.text: Wiktionary: from the root ع ن ن (ʕ n n), “appearing in view in the distance”, related to ع ي ن, the root of the eye and vision.

funFacts: عَنْ + مَا merge into عَمَّا: عَمَّا تَتَكَلَّمُ؟ (what are you talking about?) (Wiktionary).
pitfalls: Before al- it takes the helping vowel i: عَنِ الْعَمَلِ.
With pronoun endings the n doubles in the first person: عَنِّي (about me), عَنَّا (about us).
subtleties: “Far from” is بَعِيدٌ عَنْ (or مِنْ), but “near” is قَرِيبٌ مِنْ.

profile.feeling: Classrooms, school bags and the bell.

examples.tr: I go to school every morning.
The children are at school now.
There is only one school in the village.

synonyms.nuance: institute: a language school, a college
a traditional Qurʾān school for small children

etymology.text: Noun of place from the verb دَرَسَ (darasa, “to study”) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: English madrasa and Turkish medrese are this word: “the place of studying”.
pitfalls: مَدْرَسَة (madrasa, school) vs مُدَرِّسَة (mudarrisa, a female teacher): the same letters, other vowels.
The plural مَدَارِسُ is a diptote: فِي مَدَارِسَ (genitive -a without the article).
subtleties: mafʿala / mafʿal = “the place where …”: مَدْرَسَة (studying), مَكْتَب (writing → office), مَطْبَخ (cooking → kitchen).

profile.feeling: Lecture halls, campus life and diplomas.

examples.tr: My sister is a student at the university.
The university is near our house.
I study at Cairo University.
the League of Arab States

synonyms.nuance: college, faculty — a part of a university

etymology.text: The feminine of جَامِع (“gathering”), the active participle of جَمَعَ (jamaʿa, “to gather”), root ج م ع; Wiktionary gives no further etymology.

funFacts: The same root gives جَامِع (the great mosque where people gather on Friday), يَوْمُ الْجُمُعَةِ (Friday, “the day of gathering”) and جَمَاعَة (group).
pitfalls: جَامِعَة (university) vs جَامِع (a large mosque).
subtleties: Also “league, union”: جَامِعَةُ الدُّوَلِ الْعَرَبِيَّةِ, the Arab League.

profile.feeling: Jobs, offices and the daily commute.

senses.def: work — the workplace, the job: فِي الْعَمَلِ (at work)

examples.tr: My father is at work now.
I go to work by bus.
This is good work.
He is a businessman.

synonyms.nuance: work, job — the everyday spoken word
job, position (employment)

etymology.text: Verbal noun of عَمِلَ (ʕamila, “to do, to work”), root ع م ل (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Hebrew עָמָל (amal) means “toil, hard work” — the same Semitic word; Turkish amel (deed) is the Arabic one.
pitfalls: “At work” is فِي الْعَمَلِ — with the article, like فِي الْبَيْتِ.
The plural أَعْمَال means “deeds” or “business”, not “jobs” (jobs = وَظَائِف).
subtleties: مَا عَمَلُكَ؟ = What do you do for a living?

override.N;NOM;PL;INDF: Wiktionary’s table writes the plural مَكاتِب without the fatḥa on the kāf; the pattern mafāʿil is مَكَاتِب (fully vocalized)

profile.feeling: Desks, meetings and office hours.

examples.tr: My mother is at the office.
The manager’s office is over there.
The books are on the desk.

synonyms.nuance: administration, department — the institution rather than the room

etymology.text: Noun of place from the root ك ت ب (k t b, “writing”) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: “The place of writing”: كَتَبَ (to write) → كِتَاب (book) → مَكْتَب (office, desk) → مَكْتَبَة (library, bookshop). Turkish mektep (school) and mektup (letter) come from the same root.
pitfalls: مَكْتَب (office, desk) vs مَكْتَبَة (library, bookshop): the tāʾ marbūṭa makes another word.
The plural مَكَاتِبُ is a diptote.
subtleties: مَكْتَب is also “agency, bureau” in names: مَكْتَبُ سِيَاحَةٍ, مَكْتَبُ مُحَامَاةٍ (law firm).

profile.feeling: Shop windows and the corner shop.

senses.def: place, location — فِي مَحَلِّهِ (in its place, apt)

examples.tr: I buy bread at the shop.
This shop belongs to my father.
This is not the right place for that question.

synonyms.nuance: store — also online: مَتْجَرٌ إِلِكْتُرُونِيٌّ
a small shop, a traditional corner shop

etymology.text: Noun of place from حَلَّ (ḥalla, “to settle, to stop at a place”) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Its sister مَحَلَّة (quarter) became Turkish mahalle and Greek μαχαλάς, “neighbourhood”.
pitfalls: The l is doubled: مَحَلّ (maḥall); الْمَحَلُّ, فِي الْمَحَلِّ.
Two plurals: مَحَلَّات (everyday) and مَحَالّ (formal).
subtleties: مَحَلِّيّ (local) is built on it: الْوَقْتُ الْمَحَلِّيُّ = local time.

profile.feeling: Trolleys, long aisles and modern city life.

examples.tr: I buy milk at the supermarket.
The supermarket is near my house.
Is there a supermarket in the village?

synonyms.nuance: a big store — a description rather than a name
supermarket, hypermarket (lit. “central markets”) in the Gulf

etymology.text: Borrowed from English supermarket (Wiktionary).

funFacts: One international word: Greek σουπερμάρκετ, German Supermarkt, Turkish süpermarket, Russian супермаркет.
pitfalls: A loanword: careful MSA declines it like a native noun (فِي السُّوبَرْمَارْكِتِ), but in speech the ending is never heard.
Spellings vary: سُوبَرْمَارْكِت, سوبر ماركت (two words); this course gives no plural for it.
subtleties: For small daily purchases people still go to the grocer’s, الْبَقَّالَة, or the corner shop, الدُّكَّان.

profile.feeling: Noise, colours and bargaining: the souk.

examples.tr: We buy vegetables at the market.
The market is crowded on Fridays.
Market prices are high.

synonyms.nuance: bazaar (from Persian) — a covered market or a charity sale

etymology.text: From Aramaic שׁוּקָא (šūqā, “street, market”), from Akkadian sūqum (“street”), from siāqum (“to become narrow”); cognate with Hebrew שׁוּק (šuk) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Hebrew שׁוּק (shuk) is the same word, and English took souk from Arabic; its oldest ancestor, Akkadian sūqum, meant “street”.
pitfalls: سُوق is traditionally feminine, though masculine is also accepted (Wiktionary: f or m): السُّوقُ مُزْدَحِمَةٌ / مُزْدَحِمٌ.
Not سَوْق (sawq, driving).
subtleties: The plural أَسْوَاق also means “markets” in economics; in the Gulf الْأَسْوَاقُ الْمَرْكَزِيَّةُ are supermarkets.

profile.feeling: Eating out with friends and family.

examples.tr: We’re eating at a Lebanese restaurant.
This restaurant is expensive.
My brother works in a restaurant.

synonyms.nuance: canteen, snack bar

etymology.text: Noun of place (mafʿal) from the root ط ع م (“food, to eat”); Wiktionary relates it to طَعَام (food) and طَعْم (taste).

funFacts: “The eating place” — compare Greek εστιατόριο, from εστιάω, “to entertain at a feast”.
pitfalls: ط and ع side by side: maṭʿam — not *matam.
The plural مَطَاعِمُ is a diptote.
subtleties: A fast-food place is مَطْعَمُ وَجَبَاتٍ سَرِيعَةٍ.

profile.feeling: Tea, coffee, backgammon and long conversations.

examples.tr: We drink tea at the café.
My grandfather is at the café every evening.
There are many cafés in this street.

synonyms.nuance: a modern café (from French café)
in Egypt the café itself is called qahwa

etymology.text: Noun of place, denominal of قَهْوَة (qahwa, “coffee”) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: “The place of coffee”: قَهْوَة gave Turkish kahve and Greek καφές, and through Italian caffè the German Kaffee and English coffee.
pitfalls: A defective noun: مَقْهًى (maqhan) without the article, الْمَقْهَى (al-maqhā) with it — the ending does not change for case.
The plural مَقَاهٍ (maqāhin) is defective too: with the article الْمَقَاهِي.
subtleties: The traditional مَقْهًى شَعْبِيٌّ is a meeting place for men: tea, coffee, backgammon and the water pipe.

profile.feeling: Doctors, nurses and visiting hours.

examples.tr: My mother is a doctor at the hospital.
The hospital is near here.
There are many hospitals in the city.

synonyms.nuance: clinic, dispensary (smaller)
a doctor’s practice, an outpatient clinic

etymology.text: Noun of place of اِسْتَشْفَى (istašfā, “to seek a cure”), root ش ف ي: “the place for seeking a cure”. It arose at the end of the 19th century and displaced the medieval مَارِسْتَان (Wiktionary).

funFacts: The old word مَارِسْتَان (from Persian) survives mainly as “mental asylum” (Wiktionary).
pitfalls: Defective like مَقْهًى: مُسْتَشْفًى / الْمُسْتَشْفَى, with no visible case ending.
Masculine despite the final -ā: الْمُسْتَشْفَى قَرِيبٌ.
subtleties: Its plural is sound feminine: مُسْتَشْفَيَات (the ى becomes يَ).

profile.feeling: The green cross on the corner.

examples.tr: Where is the nearest pharmacy?
I buy medicine at the pharmacy.
The pharmacy is open at night.

synonyms.nuance: the old Egyptian word (from Turkish eczane, “drug house”)

etymology.text: From صَيْدَلَة (ṣaydala, “pharmacy, pharmacology”) + ـِيَّة (-iyya) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: The pharmacist is صَيْدَلِيّ or صَيْدَلَانِيّ.
pitfalls: The yāʾ is doubled: ṣaydaliyya, صَيْدَلِيَّة; plural صَيْدَلِيَّات.
subtleties: -iyya often names a place or an institution: صَيْدَلِيَّة (pharmacy), بَلَدِيَّة (town hall).

profile.feeling: Accounts, cash machines and queues.

examples.tr: I work in a bank.
The bank is closed on Friday.
Where is the bank?

synonyms.nuance: bank — the native word, in official names (مَصْرِفُ لُبْنَانَ, the Banque du Liban)

etymology.text: From Italian banco and banca, at first in the Egyptian colloquial forms بَنْكُو and بَنْكَة, later from French banque (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Italian banco is the moneychanger’s bench — and Greek τράπεζα (bank) is literally “table”: the same counter, two pictures.
pitfalls: A sukūn on n: bank, not *banak; the plural is broken: بُنُوك.
subtleties: Islamic banks and official names often prefer مَصْرِف.

profile.feeling: Stamps, parcels and queues at the counter.

senses.def: post office — مَكْتَبُ الْبَرِيدِ (the post office), مَكْتَبُ بَرِيدٍ (a post office)

examples.tr: The post office is next to the bank.
I’m going to the post office.
Is there a post office in the village?

synonyms.nuance: the post — also the post office itself: أَذْهَبُ إِلَى الْبَرِيدِ
the post office (from Italian posta), in the Levant and Egypt

etymology.text: مَكْتَب (office) + بَرِيد (post, mail). Wiktionary: بَرِيد is borrowed from Byzantine Greek βέρηδος (bérēdos, a post-horse), from Latin verēdus, from Gaulish *werēdos.

funFacts: The Arabic “post” is a Greek word: βέρηδος, the horse of the Byzantine couriers, from Latin verēdus — the Celtic word that, as paraverēdus, also became German Pferd (“horse”).
pitfalls: A construct (iḍāfa): only the second word takes the article — مَكْتَبُ الْبَرِيدِ, never *الْمَكْتَبُ الْبَرِيدِ.
The case ending goes on the first word: فِي مَكْتَبِ الْبَرِيدِ, إِلَى مَكْتَبِ الْبَرِيدِ.
subtleties: “A post office” has no article at all: مَكْتَبُ بَرِيدٍ.

profile.feeling: Platforms, timetables and departures.

senses.def: station (train, bus); also radio or petrol station

examples.tr: Where is the train station?
I’ll wait for you at the station.
The petrol station is close.

synonyms.nuance: stop, stand: مَوْقِفُ الْحَافِلَةِ (bus stop); also a car park

etymology.text: Noun of place from the verb حَطَّ (ḥaṭṭa, “to put down, to place”), root ح ط ط (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Literally “the place where one puts down (a load)” — a halt.
pitfalls: The ṭ is doubled: maḥaṭṭa, مَحَطَّة.
subtleties: مَحَطَّة is any station: trains, buses, radio, petrol (مَحَطَّةُ وَقُودٍ).

profile.feeling: Departures, arrivals and long goodbyes.

examples.tr: The airport is far from the city.
I’m at the airport now.
We’re going to the airport by taxi.

profile.synonymsNone: No synonym: مَطَار is the word everywhere; a small landing strip is مَهْبَط.

etymology.text: Noun of place from the verb طَارَ (ṭāra, “to fly”) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: “The place of flying”: طَارَ (to fly) also gives طَائِرَة (aeroplane) and طَيْر (birds).
pitfalls: مَطَار (maṭār, airport) vs مَطَر (maṭar, rain): one long vowel.
subtleties: Like مَكَان (place), it is the mafʿal pattern of a “hollow” root (ط ي ر).

profile.feeling: Traffic, shops and city life.

examples.tr: I live in this street.
The street is crowded.
There are many children in the street.

synonyms.nuance: road, way — also the way to somewhere
alley, lane

etymology.text: From the root ش ر ع (š r ʕ); it has the form of an active participle, but Wiktionary suggests that the verb شَرَعَ (“to open onto the street”) comes from the noun.

funFacts: The same root gives شَرِيعَة (law), traditionally explained as “the path (to the water)”.
pitfalls: The plural شَوَارِعُ is a diptote: فِي شَوَارِعَ (genitive -a without the article).
subtleties: Addresses use فِي: فِي شَارِعِ الْحَمْرَاءِ (on Hamra Street).

profile.feeling: Big squares, demonstrations and roundabouts.

examples.tr: The restaurant is on the square.
Tahrir Square is in Cairo.
Let’s meet on the square.
He works in the field of medicine.

synonyms.nuance: square, open space, courtyard — usual in the Levant: سَاحَةُ الشُّهَدَاءِ (Martyrs’ Square, Beirut)

etymology.text: Borrowed from an Iranian language, from Proto-Iranian *mádyanah (“middle”), from *mádyah (“middle”); compare Persian میان (miyân, “middle, between”) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: The Indo-European root of *mádyah also gives Greek μέσος, German Mitte and English middle: a square is “the middle” of the town.
pitfalls: “On the square” is فِي الْمَيْدَانِ (in), not عَلَى.
The plural مَيَادِينُ is a diptote.
subtleties: Egypt says مَيْدَان (مَيْدَانُ التَّحْرِيرِ), the Levant mostly سَاحَة.

profile.feeling: Green and shade: the public park and the garden of a house.

examples.tr: We play in the public park.
The park is far from the house.
My mother is in the garden.
There is a lemon tree in the garden of our house.

synonyms.nuance: orchard, fruit garden
park, a place for outings
garden (Egypt, Levant; a diminutive of جَنَّة, paradise)

etymology.text: Wiktionary relates it to حدق (“to surround, to enclose”): an enclosed garden.

funFacts: An enclosed garden — the same picture as Greek παράδεισος (paradise), from an Iranian word for a walled park.
pitfalls: One Arabic word for two English ones: حَدِيقَة = park and garden; the context decides.
The plural حَدَائِقُ is a diptote.
subtleties: حَدِيقَةُ الْحَيَوَانَاتِ, “the garden of the animals”, is the zoo.

profile.feeling: Crowds, lights and old quarters.

examples.tr: I live in a big city.
Cairo is an old city.
The restaurant is in the city centre.

synonyms.nuance: a small town
capital city

etymology.text: Borrowed from Aramaic מְדִינְתָּא (məḏīntā); cognate with Hebrew מְדִינָה (məḏînâ, “state”); the Arabic root م د ن was made from the noun (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Hebrew מְדִינָה (medina) means “state”, Arabic مَدِينَة “city” — the Aramaic source meant a jurisdiction, a province.
الْمَدِينَة, “the City”, is the city of the Prophet; the old quarter of North African towns is called the medina.
pitfalls: The usual plural is broken: مُدُن (mudun) — not *مَدِينَات.
subtleties: مَدَنِيّ (civil, civilian) and تَمَدُّن (urbanisation) are built on it.

profile.feeling: Fields, quiet streets and grandparents.

examples.tr: My grandmother lives in a village.
The village is near the sea.
Life in the villages is quiet.

synonyms.nuance: village (Lebanon, Syria)
village — in Egyptian place names (كَفْرُ الشَّيْخِ)

etymology.text: From Proto-West Semitic, possibly from a root of meeting and gathering; cognate with Biblical Hebrew קִרְיָה (qiryāh, “town, city”), Classical Syriac qərīṯā (“town, village”) and Phoenician qrt (“city”) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Carthage was Phoenician Qart-ḥadašt, “new town” — the same word as قَرْيَة.
أُمُّ الْقُرَى, “the mother of villages”, is an old name of Mecca.
pitfalls: The plural قُرًى (quran) is defective: with the article الْقُرَى, the same in every case.
قَرْيَة (qarya, village) vs قَرِيبَة (qarība, near, f.).
subtleties: Wiktionary notes that in older Arabic قَرْيَة could be any town; today it is a village.

profile.feeling: Homeland, borders and belonging.

examples.tr: Which country are you from?
Egypt is a big country.
I love my country.

synonyms.nuance: state — the political unit
country, land; الْبِلَادُ = the country, the homeland
homeland, fatherland — emotional

etymology.text: Wiktionary compares Ugaritic bld.

funFacts: Turkish belde (town) and belediye (municipality) come from this root (Arabic بَلْدَة, بَلَدِيَّة).
pitfalls: Two plurals: بُلْدَان (countries) and بِلَاد, which often means “the land, the country” itself.
Wiktionary also gives “town, city”: in Egypt بَلَد is one’s home town.
subtleties: “My country” is بَلَدِي; “abroad” is خَارِجَ الْبَلَدِ or فِي الْخَارِجِ.
